episode_thesis: Rich Brennan argues that 'trend follower' covers at least four different species (replicators, core diversifiers, crisis risk offset, outlier hunters) whose objectives dictate opposite design choices on breadth, momentum type, vol targeting, symmetry and speed, so most industry debates and league-table metrics talk past each other; only a long validated live track record is a universal metric. He backs the outlier-hunter case with a 68-market test in which random 30-market subsets underperform the full book 88% of the time. Niels agrees that archetypes are useful for allocators but resists absolute claims (no evidence 300-500 markets is better, asymmetric rules look like optimisation) and says short-term trend funds failed to deliver crisis alpha in 2025.

speakers.name: Rich Brennan
speakers.role: Co-host of Systematic Investor; trend follower and self-described outlier hunter (100-ish markets, static ATR-normalised small bets)
speakers.speaker_note: Captions are a single stream with no speaker labels; attribution follows the ledger and is clear from first-person statements ('I sit in the outlier hunter camp', 'my 68 market portfolio').

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers share only systematic, non-predictive rules and participation in sustained moves; their objectives differ, so even 'cut losses, let profits run' is not universal.
worldview_premises.support: Experience of the industry and many manager interviews; no data given

worldview_premises.premise: Most debates in trend following are about objectives, not facts: the same rules and data give opposite conclusions for different design goals, so advice is right only for a given archetype.
worldview_premises.support: Argument by archetype comparison (vehicle analogy: sports car vs 4x4); anecdote

worldview_premises.premise: Performance scoreboards (Sharpe, MAR, drawdown tables) homogenise different designs, hide that a high Sharpe can mean an outlier hunter is leaving upside behind, and push managers to drift into vol targeters, eroding survivability.
worldview_premises.support: Personal observation of managers morphing over time

worldview_premises.premise: The only universal evaluation metric is a long, validated live track record, because survival across many regimes applies to every style; every other metric must be matched to the archetype's purpose.
worldview_premises.support: Logical argument that survivability is the common requirement

worldview_premises.premise: A few outsized trades make the whole long-term equity curve, and it is unknowable where the next outlier will come from, but any liquid market shows fat tails over time.
worldview_premises.support: Own 68-market test (27 losers but MAR 0.8 for the book); cocoa and wheat 2022 examples

worldview_premises.premise: Under-diversification raises the role of luck: each extra market is another ticket in the fat-tail lottery and small universes magnify luck while large ones dilute it.
worldview_premises.support: Random-subset experiment on his own 68-market book

worldview_premises.premise: Breadth is not universally good: for a core diversifier it can dilute the low-correlation profile, and a crisis-offset manager should focus on markets that respond in equity drawdowns.

Design choices cascade: with about 100 markets he can use simple rules that would be less functional with fewer markets, so breadth, momentum type, sizing and rule symmetry cannot be chosen independently.

Asymmetry in rules reflects structural reality rather than prediction: commodity spikes come from supply shocks on the long side, equity collapses are violent on the short side, and speed, magnitude and persistence differ by market and direction.
worldview_premises.support: Examples: wheat 2022, natural gas 2021, equity crises; no backtest cited

steps.from: A trend follower's objective (track index, add diversification, offset crises, harvest outliers)
steps.to: Archetype with its own market count, momentum type, sizing and speed
steps.why: Each objective needs different trade-offs; a rule set perfect for one quietly sabotages another

steps.from: Archetype
steps.to: Matching evaluation metric
steps.why: Tracking error for replicators, portfolio Sharpe/correlation for diversifiers, crisis-period CAGR/convexity for crisis offset, skew and top-trade share for outlier hunters

steps.from: Wrong metric or borrowed rules from another camp
steps.to: Style drift and weaker survivability
steps.why: Managers optimise what the scoreboard rewards (e.g. outlier hunter morphing into a vol targeter)

mechanism_chains.evidence: Industry observation and interviews; no quantification.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Objectives are mixed (e.g. a 'pure trend' manager aiming for best compound return); Niels says a fifth archetype exists and managers must prove it transparently.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why breadth is the outlier hunter's edge

steps.from: Few trades produce most profit; location of next outlier unknowable
steps.to: Hold the widest feasible liquid and semi-liquid universe
steps.why: Missing the one market that goes parabolic costs more than running a tidy book

steps.from: Wide universe
steps.to: Many unprofitable markets, long dead spells (cocoa) and higher friction in small markets
steps.why: Accepted cost: one fat-tail event can outweigh years of mediocrity

steps.from: Cut the universe to 30 of 68 markets
steps.to: 88% chance of underperforming the full book on MAR; median MAR well under 0.5; weak quartile may show years of losses
steps.why: Return distribution is lopsided and skewed, so small samples usually miss the big winners and a few lucky subsets look extraordinary

mechanism_chains.evidence: 68 markets, 1 Jan 2020 to 31 Jul 2025, 3,264 trades, equal-weight; 27 of 68 markets lost money yet MAR 0.8; 300 random 30-market portfolios, only 35 (12%) reached MAR above 0.8. Single test, short sample dominated by a few events (wheat, cocoa); not validated out of sample.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Liquidity, counterparty or regulatory risk limits breadth (he will not add off-exchange or weakly regulated markets); for core diversifiers or crisis-offset managers more breadth is not better.

mechanism_chains.topic: Static small bets vs volatility targeting

steps.from: Volatility spikes mid-trend (e.g. crude vol doubles during a big uptrend)
steps.to: A vol targeter cuts the position just as the trend accelerates
steps.why: Clips the largest winners, which the outlier hunter needs

steps.from: Equal small ATR-normalised bets at entry, left unchanged
steps.to: Preserved convexity: each loss small, each winner can run fully
steps.why: Wide diversification keeps each position small, so breadth substitutes for vol targeting as the risk control

steps.from: Mandate with a vol budget and low drawdown tolerance
steps.to: Vol targeting is the right choice
steps.why: Smooths the equity curve and fits replicators and core diversifiers

mechanism_chains.evidence: Conceptual; the crude-oil case is illustrative, no test shown.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Niels notes static positions can balloon (one fund's annualised vol went from about 35 to 95) and vol targeting can also raise risk after quiet spells.

steps.from: Cross-sectional ranking trims weaker markets and tilts to leaders
steps.to: Smoother returns and controlled correlation
steps.why: Suits replicators and core diversifiers

steps.from: Same ranking applied by an outlier hunter
steps.to: Selling into strength and cutting the biggest lifetime winners
steps.why: Absolute momentum lets each trend run on its own terms

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; no conditions given beyond the archetype.

steps.from: Replicator mirrors long and short rules
steps.to: No directional bias vs the benchmark
steps.why: Keeps strategy clean and aligned to the index

steps.from: Crisis-offset: favour longs in bonds and safe-haven currencies, looser exits on those longs, tight stops on shorts in risk assets
steps.to: More convexity in equity drawdowns
steps.why: Mission is to pay off when equities fall

steps.from: Outlier hunter: commodity long side given more room; wider trailing stops on equity shorts
steps.to: Better tail capture
steps.why: Commodity spikes are supply-shock rallies; equity crashes fall violently; a commodity near historic lows has limited downside tail

mechanism_chains.evidence: Historical anecdotes (wheat 2022, natural gas 2021); no systematic test cited.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Niels warns it may simply be optimisation and that identical rules are arguably more robust.

steps.from: Faster systems
steps.to: Early loss cutting but repeated whipsaw out of long trends
steps.why: They cannot absorb interim volatility, missing the bulk of the payoff

steps.from: Long-horizon systems
steps.to: Capture multi-month moves
steps.why: Sit through volatility for the big trends

mechanism_chains.evidence: Reasoning from design philosophy; Niels adds that across time frames long-term parameters work best.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Crisis-offset objectives may justify short speeds, though Niels says 2025 evidence does not support that.

steps.from: More capital
steps.to: Add new liquid markets first rather than scale position size or add systems
steps.why: Unknown location of next outlier; any liquid market has fat tails

steps.from: System diversification
steps.to: Saturates at about 10 systems
steps.why: Ensembles deliberately decorrelate related markets such as Brent and crude

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Liquidity and counterparty or regulatory risk cap breadth.

decision_process.practice: Outlier hunter: 100 plus markets in the archetype (Rich himself says just under 100), including small illiquid ones (live cattle, rubber, milk), pure absolute momentum with no cross-sectional overlay.
decision_process.why: A few trades make the equity curve; cost of missing a fat tail exceeds cost of a messy book.

decision_process.practice: Replicators run 10-30 liquid markets with daily vol targeting and often blend cross-sectional momentum; core diversifiers use similar liquid markets and favour smoothness.
decision_process.why: Low tracking error to SG CTA index, or portfolio-level Sharpe/MAR lift.

decision_process.practice: Equal small ATR-normalised bets at entry, never resized for volatility changes.
decision_process.why: Preserve convexity; breadth keeps each bet small.

decision_process.practice: Rules may be asymmetric: more room for commodity longs, wider trailing stops on equity shorts.
decision_process.why: Improve tail capture based on structural directional profiles.

decision_process.practice: Prefer long-horizon trend systems that hold through volatility.
decision_process.why: Speed is a statement of philosophy; fast systems get chopped out of long trends.

decision_process.practice: When capital grows, add new liquid markets first; stop adding systems at about 10; avoid off-exchange or lightly regulated markets.
decision_process.why: Unknown source of next outlier; counterparty and regulatory risk not worth it.

decision_process.practice: Test breadth by random blind subsets of the universe and compare MAR distribution to the full-book benchmark rather than looking at a single backtest.
decision_process.why: Standard metrics hide survival risk from small universes.

decision_process.practice: Allocator framework: classify CTA peers into archetypes, decide which the portfolio needs, then pick the best one or two in each, judging each on its own metric.
decision_process.why: No single manager delivers all objectives.

speakers.evidence_style: Mostly design philosophy and analogy (vehicles, fisherman's net, lottery tickets) plus one Monte Carlo-style subset test on his own 68-market book; anecdotal examples for asymmetry; no out-of-sample validation and no live-track-record data shown. Stresses a long validated live record as the only universal proof.

current_views.view: Trends emerged mid-2025 after a very hard first half; equities, metals, meats and Bitcoin ('stress assets') were paying, but a sharp copper reversal hurt.
current_views.reasoning: Observation of his own book's P&L by sector.

current_views.view: Hopes the last months of 2025 bring his book back to roughly break-even for the year; cautious about declaring a good month.
current_views.reasoning: Hard year so far; sector trends improving.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host, Top Traders Unplugged; hedge fund manager and allocator-side commentator
speakers.speaker_note: Host who argues positions here (not just questions); attribution from first-person statements about his own barometer, his experience and his doubts.

worldview_premises.premise: In a fast-changing world where unimaginable moves occur (cocoa, AI disruption), non-predictive rules-based strategies are better suited than forecasting ones.
worldview_premises.support: Narrative reasoning; he calls his AI worries speculation

worldview_premises.premise: Allocators treat trend managers as interchangeable because return correlations look high, overlooking that differing designs diversify each other.
Managers will present whichever metric flatters their style, so allocators should pick the metric by the strategy's stated purpose.

Evidence does not show that more markets is better: long-tenured managers have similar rolling 10-year returns but different timing, he never saw evidence for 300-500 markets, and some top outlier-camp funds trade only 20-40.
worldview_premises.support: Own review of manager performance data (not quantified in the episode)

worldview_premises.premise: Long-term trend parameters work best across lookbacks; only crisis-offset goals justify fast speeds, and fixed 25/50/25 speed blends can now be replaced by dynamic optimisation.
worldview_premises.support: Own objective tests of time frames; not shown

worldview_premises.premise: Short-term trend funds sold as 'risk mitigation' were doubted because high-turnover systems incur slippage and costs that grow with assets; like buying VIX, the hedge is unreliable because the drivers are nuanced.

Short-term trend funds used to earn crisis alpha by capturing a vol-breakout P&L over 3-5 days without giving it back; market structure now makes those gains reverse faster, weakening the diversification benefit.
worldview_premises.support: April 2025 sell-off and 2025 index performance; cause (market structure) is a guess

worldview_premises.premise: Asymmetric rules are close to optimisation, and identical rules across markets are arguably more robust, though it is a legitimate design choice.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why short-term trend did not deliver crisis alpha in 2025

steps.from: Risk-mitigation narrative
steps.to: Large allocations to short-term trend managers
steps.why: Fast markets were said to need fast systems

steps.from: April 2025 two-day sell-off
steps.to: Gains made on two down days reversed over the next 3-5 days
steps.why: Market structure appears to reverse vol-breakout moves faster than before (his guess)

steps.from: H2 2025 choppy markets
steps.to: Short-term traders index lagged trend on a vol-adjusted basis
steps.why: Unexplained; one would expect short-term to do better

mechanism_chains.evidence: Industry index numbers for 2025 (short-term traders index -5.33% YTD vs trend index -8.77% YTD), but with a vol-adjusted claim that is not shown.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; sample is one episode of one year.

steps.from: Volatility spike
steps.to: Position cut
steps.why: Standard resize rule

steps.from: Volatility falls after correction
steps.to: Position raised again while still holding the same trade
steps.why: Path-dependent resizing; risk can rise as well as fall

steps.from: Static small bets with rising price or vol
steps.to: Position becomes a monster; annualised vol 35 -> 95 at one fund
steps.why: No resizing

mechanism_chains.evidence: One cited fund; others not named.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend following might pay in a deglobalising world

steps.from: Deglobalisation, protectionism and central-bank policy divergence
steps.to: Sustained trends in markets
steps.why: Structural regime shift he has been waiting for

steps.from: Erratic US policy noise
steps.to: Trends not yet paying
steps.why: Noise currently overpowers the signal; systems may have to treat noise as signal

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Already failing to pay out as of 2025 because of US policy noise.

decision_process.practice: Maintains a 44-market trend barometer to gauge breadth of trend strength and compares with industry indices.
decision_process.why: An apparent recovery can come from a few outlier markets outside the barometer.

decision_process.practice: Risk targeting (no resizing for ordinary vol changes but a cap on overall risk) is, he believes, what most large European CTAs now use rather than pure vol targeting.
decision_process.why: Avoids reacting to every vol move; caps the downside.

decision_process.practice: Dynamic optimisation and recalibration of speed mix instead of fixed 25/50/25 committee splits; long-term parameters preferred.
decision_process.why: Long-term parameters give best results in his tests.

decision_process.practice: Allocators should choose the evaluation metric by the strategy's purpose and bucket managers by archetype before selecting one or two per bucket.
decision_process.why: No manager delivers all objectives; marketing metrics are self-serving.

speakers.evidence_style: Allocator and practitioner scepticism: asks for evidence in performance data (rolling 10-year returns), cites industry index numbers, and distrusts absolute claims; narrative on AI and regime is explicitly speculative.

current_views.view: Trend followers are still behind equities in 2025: BTOP50 about -3.5% YTD, CTA index -7%, trend index -8.77%, short-term traders -5.33% versus MSCI World +14%, S&P 500 +10.8%, US aggregate bonds +4.7%.
current_views.reasoning: Reading of index levels as of the recording week.

current_views.view: August 2025 trend P&L is a barbell: equities and metals/meats lead, soy complex reverses, fixed income and softs are tricky.
current_views.reasoning: Sector attribution from his barometer and reports.

current_views.view: His 44-market trend barometer is weak even though the industry is up for the month, so the recovery may come from outlier markets outside it.
Still optimistic on trend following because of deglobalisation, protectionism and central-bank divergence, though it has not yet played out because US policy noise swamps trends.
current_views.reasoning: Structural-shift thesis; noise is currently the signal.

current_views.view: Short-term trend funds did not deliver crisis alpha in the April 2025 sell-off; claims that they will do so are questionable.
current_views.reasoning: Two-day gains reversed; H2 vol-adjusted underperformance.

disagreements.topic: Is wide breadth (100 plus markets, up to hundreds) the edge or just a design preference?

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: For an outlier hunter, maximum feasible breadth is the edge and non-negotiable; random 30-market subsets of his 68 beat the full book only 12% of the time; priority for new capital is more markets.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Sees no performance evidence for 300-500 markets being better; long-lived managers have similar rolling 10-year returns with different timing, and some of the best outlier-camp funds trade only 20-40 markets; asks whether there is a saturation number.

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: Asymmetry reflects structural reality and improves tail capture (commodity longs, equity shorts).

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Asymmetric rules look like optimisation; identical rules are arguably more robust, but it is the manager's choice.

disagreements.topic: Volatility targeting vs static small bets (nuance, partial disagreement)

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: Vol targeting cuts the largest winners when vol spikes mid-trend; static ATR-normalised small bets preserve convexity.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Vol-target managers also take small bets; most large firms have moved to risk targeting; static small bets can balloon (vol 35 to 95) and vol targeting can increase risk after quiet spells, so the real differences are nuances, not right or wrong.

disagreements.topic: Short-term trend as a crisis hedge

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: Faster systems get whipsawed out of long trends; short speeds are consistent only with some objectives (replicators, some core diversifiers).

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Only crisis-offset goals justify short speeds, and in 2025 short-term funds did not deliver the crisis alpha that was sold.

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: Four broad archetypes plus hybrids and niche players.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: A fifth 'pure trend' archetype exists (best long-term compound using only trend models) but must be proven transparently.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 68-market test is a single 5.5-year window (2020 to mid-2025) dominated by a few extreme moves (wheat 2022, cocoa); results for random subsets are given only as 12% of 300 samples and approximate median/25th percentile, with no confidence intervals, cost assumptions or out-of-sample check.

The comparison benchmark is the full 68-market book that Rich designed for outlier hunting, and the subsets are random rather than liquidity- or correlation-selected, so the 88% figure shows the lopsidedness of the distribution rather than that a thoughtfully chosen 30 would underperform.
Rich says breadth is capped by liquidity and regulatory risk but gives no estimate of the number of independent bets; Niels asks for it and is not given one.

Tension: Rich says his own approach is not a universal law, yet describes max breadth as 'non-negotiable' and 'oxygen'; his claim that the right design follows the objective sits alongside claims about what is better for outlier capture (breadth, absolute momentum, static sizing) that are tested only on his own book.
Rich claims scoreboards cause style drift but gives only anecdotes of managers 'morphing' into vol targeters; no named examples or numbers.
Niels's claim that large European CTAs no longer vol-target is hedged and unsourced; he also says people 'predominantly' use risk targeting with caps.
Niels's explanation for short-term underperformance (market structure) is a guess; he also says the last 6 months should have been a short-term traders' environment yet it was not.

Rich's asymmetric-rule justification (commodity long spikes, equity short crashes, limited downside when a commodity is near zero) is anecdotal and can be read as hindsight optimisation, which Niels flags.
Niels cites a fund whose annualised vol rose from about 35 to 95 under static small bets but gives no name, period or cause, so the size of the effect cannot be checked.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) No market forecast is offered. The explicit forward-looking inputs are: (1) regime inputs for trend followers (deglobalisation, protectionism, central-bank divergence) that Niels expects to eventually create persistent trends once US policy noise fades; (2) a trend barometer (his 44 markets) versus the broad CTA indices as a breadth-of-trend gauge; (3) whether short-term trend indices resume delivering vol-adjusted gains in sell-offs. Horizon is years, not months.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rich's claim reduces to a dispersion argument: if a strategy's profit comes from a few extreme tail winners, the probability that a random subset of the universe contains enough of them is low, so mean/median subset outcomes sit well below the full book. This holds mechanically for any skewed payoff and does not by itself show that 68 markets is better than, say, 50.

(reader) Both speakers agree the debates have no universal right answer, so what looks like disagreement is partly about evidence standards: Rich argues from objectives, Niels from observed performance.

(reader) For a model of manager behaviour, archetype labels give a prior on a CTA's drawdown profile and crisis behaviour (replicators track the index, outlier hunters have long dead spells and positive skew, crisis-offset managers carry negative carry), but the episode gives no data on any archetype's actual performance.

(reader) The 2025 scoreboard (trend index -8.77%, short-term -5.33%, equities strongly positive) is evidence that trend following lags in a trendless year with policy noise, not evidence on the archetype claims.

added_claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
added_claims.quote: Every additional market is another lottery ticket in the fat tail draw.
added_claims.claim: For an outlier hunter, each added market is another chance at a fat-tail winner, so breadth is the edge itself rather than a portfolio-construction nicety.
added_claims.direction: more markets raises probability of capturing outliers
added_claims.conditions: outlier-hunter design, absolute momentum, small static bets; he says not a universal law
added_claims.testable: partly - random-subset tests on own 68-market book

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: I don't think that the the volume targeting managers uh are taking big bets either. I think they're taking small bets.
added_claims.claim: Niels pushes back on Rich's framing: small bets are used on both sides, so 'small bets' does not distinguish static sizing from vol targeting.

added_claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
added_claims.quote: So the point is asymmetry is not about prediction. It's about structural reality.
added_claims.claim: Rich defends asymmetric long/short rules as a reflection of structural differences in speed, magnitude and persistence of moves by market and direction, not as a forecast.
added_claims.direction: wider room on commodity longs and equity shorts
added_claims.conditions: supply-shock commodity rallies; equity crashes; not for prices near zero
added_claims.testable: yes - historical long/short return profiles by market

added_claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
added_claims.quote: So speed is not just a technical parameter. It's a statement of philosophy.
added_claims.claim: The choice of trend-system speed reflects drawdown tolerance, patience and objective, so it should be set by the archetype rather than by a universal best lookback.
